title: A still small voice (1 Kings 19:11–13)
hookLine: not in the wind, the earthquake or the fire, but "a still small voice"

cards: What doest thou here, Elijah? The question comes to him in a cave on Horeb, the mountain of God, where he has spent the night after a long walk. He has an answer ready.
I have been very jealous for the Lord. The people have torn down your altars and killed your prophets, and I, even I only, am left, and they want my life too.
It's the answer of someone who believes he is the last one left. And instead of an argument, he's told: go out, and stand on the mountain.

teach.b: What happens next is told in a careful rhythm. A great and strong wind tears at the mountains and breaks the rocks in pieces. "But the LORD was not in the wind."
After the wind, an earthquake; the Lord was not in the earthquake.

teach.h: NOT IN THE EARTHQUAKE, NOT IN THE FIRE.
teach.b: After the earthquake, a fire; the Lord was not in the fire. Three times the noise builds, and three times: not there.
And then, in the King James and the Jewish Publication Society words alike, "a still small voice." Elijah hears it, wraps his face in his cloak, and steps to the mouth of the cave.
This is the prophet of Carmel, the man of fire. Fire fell at his word. And now he's shown that God is not in the fire.
The Hebrew phrase, kol demamah dakah, is hard to translate, and readers have heard it different ways: a still small voice, a quiet whisper, even a sound of thin silence. The text doesn't settle it.
Whatever it was, it was quiet enough to miss if you were waiting for thunder. One more detail, an honest one.
The voice asks the very same question again, what doest thou here, Elijah, and Elijah gives the very same answer, word for word. The quiet doesn't magically fix him.
But in that quiet he receives his next instructions, and learns he is not as alone as he thought. The wind really did break rocks. It just wasn't where God was speaking.

how: Jews read Elijah at Horeb as part of the book of Kings and as a haftarah, and the phrase kol demamah dakah appears in the Unetaneh Tokef prayer of the High Holy Days.

o: stillness: a hush so quiet it's easy to miss
a whirlwind that lifts someone into the sky
thunder: a loud sign rolling over a mountain

games.q: a still small voice — tap the pairs.
p: the Lord was not in it
still and small, after the fire
he wraps his face in it

s: God spoke to Elijah from the fire
the text says the Lord was not in the fire.
after the voice, Elijah gave the same answer as before
he repeats his words: I, even I only, am left.
the Hebrew phrase has one fixed meaning
readers hear kol demamah dakah as a quiet voice, a whisper, or a thin silence.

games.q: you're on the mountain. a wind breaks the rocks, an earthquake shakes the ground, a fire blazes. what comes next?
games.why: the text says the Lord was not in the wind, the earthquake or the fire. after them all: a still small voice.

practice: Put the phone out of reach, and first notice the loud things, traffic, a fan, the noise in your own head, naming each one and letting it pass the way the wind, the earthquake and the fire passed.
Then listen underneath, to your breath, the room itself, a quiet you usually talk over, staying at the mouth of the cave without waiting for anything to happen.

wordCard.voice: Demamah. The Hebrew for stillness, inside the phrase Elijah heard after the wind, the earthquake and the fire. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: the phrase in 1 Kings 19:12, rendered a still small voice.

carryVoice: Your line: quiet enough to miss. The noise was real; the voice was somewhere else. See you tomorrow.

sources.q: but the LORD was not in the wind
